blocks.text: A pediatric cervical collar is a medical device used to limit movement of the cervical spine when a neck injury is suspected or confirmed.

It is commonly used as one component of spinal motion restriction during trauma assessment and transfer. It does not independently immobilize the entire spine, and correct sizing, manual stabilization when indicated, and appropriate handling remain essential.
Classification: Emergency and trauma-support equipment.
Common settings: Emergency departments, ambulances, trauma units, and pediatric resuscitation areas.
Key identification feature: A shaped support that fits around the neck, with chin and occipital support designed to restrict cervical movement.
1. Rigid cervical collar
Provides structural support and limits some cervical movement. It is commonly used when cervical spine injury is suspected and a collar is indicated.
2. Adjustable cervical collar
Allows the height or fit to be adjusted to accommodate different neck dimensions, according to the manufacturer's instructions.
3. Soft cervical collar
Provides gentle support but does not provide the same movement restriction as a rigid trauma collar. It is not a substitute for an indicated rigid collar in trauma care.

Important OSCE distinction: A cervical collar is not routinely applied to every injured child. Its use depends on the mechanism of injury, examination findings, clinical risk, and the applicable pediatric trauma protocol. Unnecessary immobilization can itself cause harm.
A pediatric cervical collar may be used when cervical spine injury is suspected and spinal motion restriction is indicated.

items.text: Blunt trauma with concerning neck pain or tenderness.
Suspected cervical spine fracture or ligament injury.
Significant trauma with an unreliable examination, depending on the clinical protocol.
Altered consciousness following trauma when cervical spine injury cannot be excluded.
Selected situations during transfer or extrication where spinal motion restriction is indicated.

blocks.text: A collar is only one component of spinal motion restriction. Appropriate handling, head and neck support, assessment, and transfer techniques are also important.
Children have age-specific anatomical and physiological considerations. A child should not automatically be managed using an adult collar or adult clearance criteria.
1. Chin support
Supports the mandible and helps maintain the intended collar position without forcing the neck into an abnormal posture.
2. Occipital support
Supports the back of the head and helps limit cervical movement when the collar is correctly fitted.
3. Height adjustment mechanism
Allows the collar to be adjusted to the appropriate height for the child's anatomy, where supported by the device.
4. Fastening straps
Secure the collar around the neck while maintaining the intended fit.
5. Padding and contact surfaces
Improve comfort and reduce direct pressure, although prolonged collar use can still cause skin injury.

blocks.text: Examiner tip: Never claim that a cervical collar completely immobilizes the cervical spine. It reduces some movement and must be used as part of an appropriate trauma-management strategy.

blocks.text: Young children have a relatively large occiput compared with their body size. When lying flat, this can cause the neck to flex forward. A collar should not force the head into a position that compromises alignment or breathing.
Use an age-appropriate support and positioning strategy under the relevant pediatric trauma protocol.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to apply a pediatric cervical collar: step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: Assess airway, breathing, and circulation first. If cervical spine injury is suspected, minimize unnecessary neck movement and maintain manual stabilization when indicated.
Do not delay lifesaving airway or resuscitation interventions to apply a collar.
Choose a pediatric collar that matches the child's anatomy. Follow the device's sizing guide and check that the collar is suitable for the child's neck length and jaw position.

content_groups.group_title: Step 3: Assess head and neck alignment

blocks.text: Observe the child's natural alignment. Avoid forcing the neck into a neutral position if there is pain, resistance, deformity, or concern that movement could worsen an injury.
In infants and young children, account for the prominent occiput and the possibility of flexion when supine.
Use the manufacturer's specified landmarks and adjustment method. Confirm the collar height before application when possible.
With appropriate stabilization maintained by a trained team member, position the collar according to the device instructions.
Ensure that the chin support sits correctly and that the collar does not obstruct the mouth, compress the throat, or force the head into an abnormal position.
Fasten the collar securely without overtightening. Check that it remains correctly positioned and does not migrate.

items.text: Airway patency and breathing.
Comfort and distress.
Head and neck alignment.
Skin pressure points.
Neurological findings, where assessment is possible.

blocks.text: If the collar compromises the airway or worsens alignment, correct the problem immediately while maintaining appropriate stabilization.

Continue the trauma assessment and arrange appropriate imaging or cervical spine clearance according to the child's clinical risk and local protocol. A collar must not substitute for clinical assessment.
Document the reason for application, collar type and size, fit, neurovascular findings where relevant, and the ongoing plan for reassessment and removal.
A cervical collar may be inappropriate or require modification when it worsens alignment, compromises the airway, or cannot fit the child's anatomy safely.

items.text: Airway emergency: Airway management takes priority. Use appropriate manual stabilization where possible, but do not allow a collar to prevent lifesaving intervention.
Abnormal head posture or deformity: Do not force the neck into a predetermined position.
Prolonged use: Reassess the need for the collar and remove it when cervical spine clearance criteria are met under the appropriate protocol.
Infants: Ensure that collar dimensions and positioning accommodate the relatively large occiput and short neck.

blocks.text: A cervical collar is a supportive device, not a diagnostic instrument. The assessment focuses on fit, positioning, skin integrity, airway safety, and the child's clinical condition.

blocks.text: Important: A normal examination while wearing a collar does not exclude cervical spine injury. Clinical clearance should follow an appropriate pediatric trauma protocol.
Infants
Have a relatively large occiput and short neck. Standard adult positioning may produce neck flexion, so age-appropriate support and careful alignment are essential.
Young children
Need a collar sized for their anatomy rather than an adult collar tightened to fit. Reassess fit and comfort after application.
Older children and adolescents
May use appropriately sized pediatric or adult devices depending on body dimensions and manufacturer guidance. Apply pediatric trauma assessment and clearance criteria.

A cervical collar is not routinely required for every child with minor trauma.
If spinal injury is suspected, maintain appropriate motion restriction during transfers and examination.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a pediatric cervical collar?
A device used to restrict some cervical spine movement when indicated as part of spinal motion restriction in a child with suspected or confirmed cervical spine injury.
Q2. Does a cervical collar completely immobilize the neck?
No. It limits some movement but does not completely immobilize the cervical spine. Appropriate handling and other motion-restriction measures may be required.
Q3. Why must pediatric collars be correctly sized?
An incorrectly sized collar may fail to provide appropriate support, cause abnormal alignment, compromise the airway, or create pressure injuries.
Q4. What is the importance of the occiput in infants?
The relatively large occiput can cause neck flexion when an infant lies flat. Positioning must account for this anatomy.
Q5. What should you assess before application?
Airway, breathing, circulation, the mechanism of injury, cervical spine risk, neck alignment, and the suitability of the collar.
Q6. Name four complications of cervical collar use.
Pressure injury, airway compromise, pain or agitation, and difficulty swallowing.
Q7. What would you do if the collar compromised the child's airway?
I would prioritize airway management, correct the collar-related problem, and maintain appropriate stabilization as feasible while following the emergency protocol.
Q8. Should a collar be applied to every child after trauma?
No. Application depends on clinical risk and the relevant pediatric trauma protocol.
Q9. How do you know whether the collar is correctly fitted?
The collar is appropriately sized, securely positioned, and maintains the intended support without forcing alignment, obstructing breathing, or creating excessive pressure.
Q10. When should the collar be removed?
When cervical spine injury has been appropriately excluded or the collar is no longer indicated, following the relevant clinical clearance protocol.
Using an adult collar on a small child
Select a device appropriate to the child's dimensions and anatomy.
Forcing the head into neutral alignment
Avoid forced positioning when pain, deformity or resistance is present.
Ignoring airway compromise
Reassess breathing immediately after application and prioritize airway management.
Assuming the collar eliminates all movement
Remember that it is only one component of spinal motion restriction.
Leaving the collar on without review
Reassess the indication and arrange appropriate cervical spine clearance.

Examiner tip: Demonstrate correct sizing, alignment, securement, airway reassessment, and recognition of pediatric anatomical differences. Mention that airway and circulation take priority over collar application.

Identification: Pediatric cervical support device.
Purpose: Limits some cervical movement during indicated trauma care.
Priority: Airway, breathing, and circulation.
Key pediatric issue: Large occiput and short neck in infants.
Complications: Pressure injury, airway compromise, pain, and swallowing difficulty.
Critical limitation: Does not completely immobilize the cervical spine.
Follow-up: Reassess the child and arrange appropriate cervical spine clearance.
